summary: Provides guidelines for developers of Next Hop Resolution Protocol clients, defining how the NHC code should interact with the TCP/IP stack of the host operating system. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a how-to for programmers building the part of a computer that asks where to send messages next on a shared network.

subtitle: How to implement protocol clients for ATM shortcut routing

tldr.problem: ATM networks can offer shortcuts for IP traffic, but implementing clients to use them requires careful management of network paths and caching decisions that differ from traditional routing.
tldr.mechanism: The NHC must test whether destinations are local or remote, query a server for shortcuts, cache both successful shortcuts and rejected requests, and allow applications to override default path selection.
tldr.outcome: Developers can build clients that enable ATM shortcut paths for improved performance while falling back to standard routing when shortcuts are unavailable.

today: RFC 2583 is an Informational document from May 1999 and is still the primary guide for NHC developers working with ATM shortcut implementations. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2583 provides guidelines for developers building Next Hop Client (NHC) software that runs on computers connected to ATM networks. The NHC replaces traditional ATMARP code and enables clients to request shortcuts through ATM networks when sending traffic to remote destinations.

In a standard ATM setup called Classical IP, all inter-subnet traffic must flow through routers. NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol) allows clients to ask a server whether a direct ATM connection (shortcut) is available instead. The NHC must manage this decision-making process and maintain a cache of both successful shortcuts and failed attempts to avoid repeatedly asking when no shortcut exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally, messages between different parts of a network go through a router. But ATM networks can set up direct connections called shortcuts. An NHC is software that asks a server if a shortcut is available, then uses it if one exists.

sections.title: How IP Processing Works
sections.content:
When an application sends data, IP first checks a routing table to see if the destination is in the same local subnet (LIS, or Logical IP Subnet) or in a different one. For local destinations, the system looks up the ATM address using an ARP-like table. For remote destinations, IP extracts the next-hop router address from the routing table.

In traditional Classical IP over ATM, local packets use direct ATM connections and remote packets always flow through routers. The NHC changes this by allowing remote destinations to also attempt shortcut paths, overriding the normal local/remote test in the IP routing table.
sections.plainLanguage: IP checks if a destination is nearby or far away. If far, it normally sends the message to a router. But an NHC can ask if a shortcut exists first, even for far destinations.

sections.title: NHC Functions and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies four key functions an NHC must perform: test whether a destination is local using the same rules as ATMARP; if remote, send an NHRP message to the Next Hop Server asking for a shortcut; if a shortcut is available, cache the IP-to-ATM mapping; if no shortcut exists, cache this negative result to avoid repeated requests.

Additionally, the NHC must allow user applications to explicitly request or forbid shortcuts for specific connections. Like traditional ARP and ATMARP, cached information must be maintained using timers that expire old entries, and administrators must be able to manually examine and modify the cache.
sections.plainLanguage: An NHC must ask whether a shortcut exists, remember the answer (yes or no), let users override the choice, and clean up old information over time.

sections.title: Caching Shortcuts and Rejections
sections.content:
The NHC cache must be fast because it is checked on every packet, must be indexed by destination IP address rather than next-hop router address, and must store both positive responses (ACK, meaning a shortcut is available) and negative responses (NAK, meaning no shortcut exists) for the duration specified in the NHRP response.

The RFC identifies six possible locations to store this state: in the ARP table, in the IP routing table, in an ATM MIB structure, in a TCP Process Control Block, in socket structures, or in a newly defined table. It recommends supporting both global (per-system) defaults and per-process overrides, allowing, for example, DNS queries to use the routed path while FTP sessions use shortcuts.
sections.plainLanguage: The cache needs to remember both successful shortcuts and failed attempts, with different applications able to prefer different paths. DNS might prefer a standard route while file transfer might prefer shortcuts.

sections.title: Application Control of Path Selection
sections.content:
The RFC recommends creating a new socket option that allows applications to specify one of five path-selection modes: USE_SYSTEM_DEFAULT (follow system configuration), USE_SHORT_CUT (demand a shortcut or fail), TRY_SHORT_CUT (use a shortcut if available, else fall back to routed), USE_ROUTED_PATH (never attempt shortcuts), or TRY_ROUTED_PATH (do not create new shortcuts, use routed path only).

This design gives application programmers and administrators flexibility to tune network behavior for different workloads. It also enables management operations like ping and traceroute to use either path type as specified, which is important for network troubleshooting and verification.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications get options: use shortcuts if available, demand a shortcut, forbid shortcuts, or let the system choose. This lets network managers fine-tune performance for each type of traffic.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three main security threats: address spoofing at the IP or ATM layer that could hijack a connection or service; denial-of-service attacks that could flood the NHS with signaling messages or register false IP-to-ATM mappings; and the fact that shortcut paths bypass the border router where a firewall or other security function normally resides.

Mitigation strategies include limiting the scope of the ATM routing domain to only trusted hosts, adding security features to the NHC host itself, allowing the NHS to evaluate security policies when approving shortcuts, or combining these approaches. These measures help prevent untrusted external attackers from exploiting the shortcut mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Shortcuts bypass routers where firewalls normally check traffic. The system should trust only local ATM hosts, check requests carefully, and protect against fake address claims.
